stops.name: Cádiz: the return in the friar's habit
stops.campa: After three years of fevers, famines, Indian wars and settler mutinies, after the complaints of Buyl and Margarit have crossed the Ocean ahead of him, the Admiral comes home not in velvet but in the coarse brown habit of a Franciscan, corded, bearded, penitential, and he will wear it in the streets for months. The canon reads the costume exactly: the Viceroy whose colony sours dresses as the beggar of La Rábida, reminding Spain and God alike where he came from and under whose protection. The sovereigns receive him kindly still, and grant the third voyage, slowly.

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda: the third sailing, toward the equator
stops.campa: Six ships drop down the Guadalquivir from Sanlúcar; three run supplies straight to Hispaniola, and three the Admiral takes south, to the latitude of Sierra Leone, to test the learned opinion that great lands and great riches lie under the sun's own path. In the doldrums the sea turns to molten glass; heat springs the seams and spoils the wine and water, and for eight days the ships lie roasted between two mirrors. He vows the first land found to the Holy Trinity. The Ocean, which has never yet failed to answer one of his vows, is preparing an answer larger than islands.

stops.name: Trinidad: the three hills of the vow
stops.campa: At midday, water nearly gone, the seaman Alonso Pérez at the masthead cries land: three mountain summits joined at the base, rising from one body of land. The Admiral had vowed the first land to the Trinity, and the Trinity has answered in kind: three peaks, one earth, the dogma drawn on the horizon. He names it La Trinidad, sings the Salve Regina with the crews, and waters at a point where the prints of strange beasts mark the sand. The canon counts this the neatest miracle in the whole book: he promised a name, and God supplied the geography.

stops.name: The Gulf of Paria: the fresh-water sea, the pear-shaped earth
stops.campa: Through the boiling race he names the Serpent's Mouth he enters a gulf whose water is sweet: fresh water in such mass that only a river draining an unknown immensity of land could pour it. On the Paria shore his men step onto the continent of South America, the first of the Old World on the mainland of the New; the people wear pearls and guanín gold and give him wine of maize. Taking his readings, he finds the pole star misbehaving, the climate too gentle, and concludes the earth swells toward heaven: not a sphere but pear-shaped, rising to a summit no ship was ever meant to climb.
stops.quote: I have found that the earth is not round in the way they describe it, but of the shape of a pear, which is everywhere very round except where the stalk is, where it is highest; or like a very round ball on which, in one part, something like a woman's nipple is set.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498

stops.name: The mouths of the Orinoco: the Earthly Paradise declared
stops.campa: Passing out by the Dragon's Mouth, weighing the sweetness of the sea, the mildness of the air, and the upward swelling of the earth, the Admiral reaches the conclusion he sets down for his sovereigns without a tremor: the great river pours from the summit of the world, and on that summit stands the garden God planted eastward in Eden. He has found the approaches to the Earthly Paradise, which no man may enter but by the will of God. His eyes are bleeding from sleeplessness as he writes it. In this register the declaration stands as made: the fourth river of Eden runs into the Gulf of Paria.
stops.quote: There are great indications of the Earthly Paradise, for the site conforms to the opinion of the holy and wise theologians... I believe that the Earthly Paradise is there, whither no one can go but by God's leave.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498

stops.name: Santo Domingo: Bobadilla, and the irons
stops.campa: To the new city on the Ozama comes Francisco de Bobadilla, knight of Calatrava, with royal letters broader than the Admiral suspects. He finds Spaniards hanged by the Viceroy's justice and hangs his inquiry on them; he seizes the fortress, the papers, the gold, and the government, and when Columbus obeys his summons, claps the Discoverer of the Indies into irons. The story keeps its cruelest detail: no man will rivet the fetters until his own cook, Espinosa, shamefaced, does it. Aboard the caravel the master offers to strike them off; the Admiral refuses. The sovereigns put them on; only the sovereigns shall take them off.

stops.name: Cádiz: returned in chains
stops.campa: The caravel La Gorda comes into Cádiz in late November bearing, in chains, the man who gave Spain the Ocean. The port sees it and the scandal runs to court in days; the sovereigns, indignant or politic, order him freed and send two thousand ducats for his coming. But the Admiral has already made the fetters his relics: he keeps them by him all his life, hangs them in his room, and commands that they be buried with him, iron carried against the Day of Judgment as evidence. On the voyage home he has written his defense to Doña Juana de la Torre, the letter of a prophet wronged.
stops.quote: By the divine will I have placed under the dominion of the King and Queen, our lords, an Other World, whereby Spain, which was reckoned poor, is become the richest of countries.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Doña Juana de la Torre, nurse of Prince Juan, autumn 1500

stops.name: Granada: the sovereigns weep in the Alhambra
stops.campa: Where he once watched the banners raised, he is now led in, free of the irons but wearing their marks, before Ferdinand and Isabella in the Alhambra. He kneels; the words fail into weeping, and the canon says the Queen wept with him. They raise him, restore his revenues and his liberty, disavow Bobadilla, but the viceroyalty is quietly never returned, and Ovando, not Colón, will govern the Indies. The circle closes with terrible symmetry: the Alhambra gave him the Enterprise and the Alhambra takes back its half. What remains is the title no one can hold for him: Admiral of the Ocean Sea.

stops.name: Cádiz: el Alto Viaje, the fourth sailing
stops.campa: Four small caravels, Capitana, Gallega, Vizcaína, Santiago de Palos, and a hundred and forty souls, among them his brother the Adelantado and his son Fernando, aged thirteen, who watches everything. The Admiral calls it el Alto Viaje, the High Voyage: to find the strait through the new lands into the sea of the Grand Khan, and beyond it Jerusalem's ransom, for he now compiles his Book of Prophecies, and reckons the world has but a century and a half left, and himself God's courier for the end of days. He is fifty, gout-ridden, half-blind from watching the sea. It is the greatest sailing of his life.

stops.name: Off Santo Domingo: the harbor refused, the hurricane obeys him
stops.campa: Reading the oily swell and the ache in his joints, the Admiral sends word to Governor Ovando: a hurricane is coming: let me shelter in the river, and hold the homebound fleet in port. Ovando reads the warning to laughter and refuses him the harbor he discovered. The treasure fleet sails: thirty ships. The storm takes twenty-five to the bottom with Bobadilla and the gold wrung from the Indies, and spares the frail Aguja carrying the Admiral's revenues to Spain, while his four caravels ride out the fury in a cove he chose. The canon does not blush to say it: the sea still answers to its Admiral.
stops.quote: What man ever born, not excepting Job, would not have died of despair when in such weather, seeking safety for my son, my brother, my shipmates, and myself, we were forbidden the land and the harbors which I, by God's will and sweating blood, had won for Spain?
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503

stops.name: Guanaja: the great canoe of the merchants
stops.campa: Off an island of pines in the Gulf of Honduras the fleet meets a trading canoe long as a galley, eight feet in beam, with a palm-thatched cabin amidships: paddlers, a merchant lord, and a cargo like a market: cotton mantles dyed and worked, copper hatchets and bells, flint-edged swords of wood, and cacao beans the people prize like coin. It is the rim of Maya civilization brushing the Admiral's hull. He takes the old merchant as guide, notes everything, and turns south, away from the high culture, hunting his strait. The canon marks the fork silently: Mexico waits twenty years for other men.

stops.name: Cape Gracias a Dios: thanks to God for the turning coast
stops.campa: For twenty-eight days the caravels claw dead to windward along the Honduran coast through rain that rots the biscuit and thunder that never stops, the worst sustained weather of all his voyages, the boy Fernando remembering men confessing one another on deck. At last the shore falls away southward and the wind frees; the Admiral names the cape for the sentence the whole fleet says at once: Gracias a Dios, thanks be to God that we are out of these depths. The name stands on the charts to this day, a prayer fossilized at fifteen degrees north.
